prompt: In one sentence: what is the fundamental architectural difference between a CPU and a GPU, and what workload does each favor?

src.ref: Ch.1 Introduction — latency- vs throughput-oriented design

reveal: The gist: a **CPU** is built to make a few threads finish fast; a **GPU** is built to run thousands of simple threads at once. A CPU spends its transistors on control logic, branch prediction, and big caches, so it is **latency-optimized** — good at branchy, sequential, one-thing-after-another work. A GPU spends them on thousands of simple **ALUs** (arithmetic units) that share control logic and run in parallel, so it is **throughput-optimized** — good at wide, regular, data-parallel work: the same operation over huge arrays, which is exactly what matrix multiply is. **Tell:** few-fast-threads (CPU) vs many-slow-threads (GPU).

prompt: What is a warp, and what is warp divergence? Why does an if/else inside a kernel cost more than on a CPU?

src.ref: Ch.4 Compute architecture and scheduling — warps and SIMT

reveal:
Gist: a **warp** is a pack of 32 GPU threads that all run the *same* instruction at the same moment; **warp divergence** is what happens when an if/else forces them to disagree.

GPUs execute in **SIMT** style — Single Instruction, Multiple Threads: the hardware issues one instruction and all 32 threads in the warp run it in lockstep, each on its own data. When a branch sends some threads down the `if` and others down the `else`, the warp **diverges**, and the hardware cannot run both paths together. It runs them **serially** — first the `if` path with the `else` threads switched off (masked), then the `else` path with the `if` threads masked. So a branch that splits a warp roughly **doubles** that section's cost.

A CPU never pays this: its branch predictor just guesses one direction and keeps going. **The tell:** to keep a GPU fast, arrange data so all threads in a warp take the same path — divergence, not arithmetic, is the hidden cost of branches on a GPU.

prompt: What is memory coalescing and why does it dominate GPU kernel performance? Connect it to CPU cache lines.

src.ref: Ch.5 Memory architecture and data locality — coalesced global memory access

reveal:
Gist: **memory coalescing** is when the 32 threads of a warp read *neighbouring* addresses, so the hardware satisfies them all with one wide memory fetch instead of many.

When a warp's threads touch consecutive addresses, the hardware **merges** those accesses into a single wide transaction — that is coalescing. Scattered, jumbled addresses force many separate transactions, and each transaction hauls a fixed-size chunk whether you use all of it or one byte, so most of the fetch is wasted. It is the same idea as a **CPU cache line** — the CPU pulls 64 bytes even if you asked for one — but amplified, because a GPU is **bandwidth-bound**: its speed is set by how many *useful* bytes per second it moves, so wasted bytes convert directly into lost throughput.

**The tell:** getting the access pattern right — thread `i` reads element `i`, so a warp sweeps a contiguous run — often matters more than the arithmetic inside the kernel.

prompt: Name the GPU memory hierarchy from fastest to slowest and state what shared memory is FOR.

src.ref: Ch.5 Memory architecture and data locality — the memory hierarchy

reveal:
Gist: the GPU's memory runs from tiny-and-instant to huge-and-slow, and **shared memory** is the one level you manage by hand to dodge the slow trips.

Fastest to slowest: **registers** (private to each thread, fastest) → **shared memory / L1** (on-chip, shared within one thread block) → **L2** (on-chip, shared across the whole device) → **global memory**, the off-chip **HBM/DRAM** (High-Bandwidth Memory / DRAM — the big pool of VRAM) and the slowest. **Shared memory is a programmer-managed cache**: unlike an automatic CPU cache, you explicitly load data into it and decide what stays.

Its job: let a thread **block** (a cooperating group of threads on one chip unit) load a **tile** — a small sub-block of data — from global memory *once*, then reuse it many times on-chip. **The tell:** that reuse is exactly what turns matrix multiply from **bandwidth-bound** (waiting on memory) into **compute-bound** (limited by math) — so any kernel that re-reads the same global data should stage it in shared memory first.

prompt: Define arithmetic intensity and use the roofline model to explain why a large matmul is compute-bound while an elementwise add is memory-bound.

src.ref: Ch.1 A Brief Intro to Roofline Analysis

reveal:
Gist: **arithmetic intensity** is how much math you do per byte you fetch — FLOPs per byte — and the **roofline** model says that one number predicts whether you are limited by the math units or by memory.

A **FLOP** is one floating-point operation; intensity = FLOPs performed ÷ bytes moved from memory. Roofline: achievable performance = min(**peak FLOPs**, intensity × **memory bandwidth**). Below a hardware-specific intensity you are **memory-bound** (starved for bytes); above it you are **compute-bound** (starved for math). An **elementwise add** over n numbers does ~1 FLOP per ~12 bytes moved — two reads and one write of 4-byte floats — a tiny intensity, so it is memory-bound. An **n×n matrix multiply** does ~2n³ FLOPs while moving only ~12n² bytes (three n×n matrices of 4-byte floats), so its intensity *grows with n*; large matmuls sit far to the right and become compute-bound.

**The tell — why kernel fusion helps:** a chain of cheap ops is all memory-bound, so merging them removes the memory round-trips between them and reclaims the wasted bandwidth.

prompt: Explain tiled matrix multiplication: what problem does tiling solve, and roughly how much does it reduce global-memory traffic?

src.ref: Ch.5 Memory architecture and data locality — tiled matrix multiplication

reveal:
Gist: **tiling** fixes matmul's memory problem — instead of re-reading rows and columns from slow memory over and over, load a small square **tile** into fast on-chip memory once and reuse it.

Naive matmul fetches each input element from **global memory** about O(n) times, because every output element re-reads a full row and a full column, so the kernel is bandwidth-starved. Tiling loads a **T×T tile** (a T-by-T sub-block, T the tile width) of each input into **shared memory** once; then every thread in the block reuses that tile for T **multiply-accumulates** (multiply-then-add, the core matmul step) before moving on. Global-memory traffic drops by roughly a **factor of T**.

**The tell:** this is the canonical trade of on-chip memory for off-chip bandwidth — the *same* bet as keeping weights in SRAM right next to the compute on Cerebras/Tenstorrent hardware. Reuse data while it is on-chip; every extra reuse is a global fetch you did not pay for.

prompt: What is occupancy, and why is maximizing it NOT always the goal?

src.ref: Ch.4 Compute architecture and scheduling — occupancy and resource limits

reveal:
Gist: **occupancy** is how full a compute unit is — the fraction of its warp slots actually in use — and cranking it to the maximum is *not* the goal.

It is the ratio of **active warps** on a **streaming multiprocessor** (SM — one of the GPU's parallel compute units) to the most that SM can hold. High occupancy helps **hide memory latency**: while some warps wait on a slow fetch, others have work to do, so the math units stay busy. But it is not an end in itself — **registers** and **shared memory** are finite and split among the resident threads, so raising occupancy hands each thread fewer of them. That can force **register spilling** (overflowing registers into slow memory) or starve the **tiling** that made the kernel fast in the first place.

**The tell:** a lower-occupancy kernel with good data reuse routinely beats a high-occupancy one with poor reuse — occupancy is a means to hide latency, not a score to maximize.

prompt: What is the CUDA execution hierarchy — thread, block, grid — and what can synchronize with what?

src.ref: Ch.3 Multidimensional grids and data — grids, blocks, threads

reveal:
Gist: a CUDA kernel runs as a three-level nest — a **grid** of **blocks** of **threads** — and the key rule is that threads inside a block can coordinate, but blocks cannot.

Launching a kernel spawns a **grid** (the whole launch) made of thread **blocks**, each block holding many **threads**. Threads in one block run on the same **streaming multiprocessor** (SM — one parallel compute unit), share its fast **shared memory**, and can line up at a barrier with `__syncthreads()` (wait here until every thread in the block arrives). **Blocks are independent by design**: within a single kernel launch there is no general way to synchronize across blocks, because the hardware may run them in any order, at different times, or not simultaneously at all.

**The tell:** that block independence is exactly what lets the *same* code scale across a small GPU or a huge one — and it means cross-block coordination needs either a **separate kernel launch** or **atomics** on global memory, never a `__syncthreads()` across blocks.

prompt: What problem does FlashAttention solve, and what is the key insight?

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Optimizing Attention

reveal:
Gist: **FlashAttention** makes attention faster without changing its math — by never writing the giant attention matrix to slow memory.

Standard attention builds the full **N×N attention matrix** (N = sequence length; every token scored against every token) in **HBM**, the off-chip high-bandwidth memory, so **memory traffic** — not arithmetic — dominates, and that memory grows **quadratically** with sequence length. FlashAttention never materializes that matrix: it **tiles** the work, loading blocks of the Q, K, V matrices (queries, keys, values) into on-chip **SRAM**, computing partial attention there, and stitching the pieces with an **online (streaming) softmax** — a running normalization that rescales its partial sums as new blocks arrive, so the result stays exact without ever seeing a whole row at once.

**The tell:** the same output with **linear** memory and far less HBM traffic — a pure memory-movement win, not a math change. It is the canonical **IO-aware** kernel: optimize the data movement, and the FLOPs take care of themselves.

see.label: Dao et al. — FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness

prompt: What is kernel fusion and why does it help so much for elementwise chains?

src.ref: Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr — Bandwidth (operator fusion)

reveal:
Gist: **kernel fusion** merges several operations into one GPU kernel so the in-between results never leave fast memory.

Run as separate kernels, a chain like x → add → multiply → **relu** (a simple activation) reads and writes the whole tensor **three times** through slow **global memory** — once per op. **Fused** into a single kernel, the intermediates stay in registers or shared memory, so it reads once and writes once. Because elementwise ops have tiny **arithmetic intensity** (little math per byte), they are entirely **bandwidth-bound** — runtime is set by memory traffic — so cutting that traffic ~3× cuts runtime ~3×.

**The tell:** this is why `torch.compile`, **XLA**, and **TensorRT** pour so much effort into fusion — for memory-bound elementwise chains, fewer memory round-trips is almost the whole game.

prompt: Why is LLM training compute-bound while single-stream inference is memory-bound?

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — LLM Inference Bottlenecks (prefill vs decode)

reveal:
Gist: **training** reuses each loaded weight across a whole batch, so it is limited by math; single-stream **inference** reuses each weight once, so it is limited by memory.

Training processes large **batches**, so a weight streamed once from memory feeds many samples — **arithmetic intensity** (math per byte) is high and the GPU's **FLOPs** are the ceiling: **compute-bound**. **Autoregressive** inference (generate one token, feed it back, repeat) emits **one token at a time**: to produce it you must stream the **entire weight matrix** from memory to do what is essentially a **matrix-vector** product, reusing each weight exactly once. Intensity is near 1 FLOP per byte, so you are **memory-bandwidth-bound** and the math units sit idle.

**The tell:** because single-stream decode wastes the FLOPs and pays for the bytes, every inference trick targets *memory* — **quantization**, **batching**, **speculative decoding**, and keeping weights in **SRAM**.

prompt: What does quantization do for inference, and why does it help more than the FLOP count suggests?

src.ref: Ch.5 Techniques — Quantization

reveal:
Gist: **quantization** stores the model's numbers in fewer bits, and it speeds inference far more than the FLOP count would suggest — because inference is bottlenecked on memory, not math.

It keeps weights (and sometimes activations) in **lower precision** — **INT8**, **FP8**, or **INT4** (8-, 8-, and 4-bit) instead of **FP16/FP32** (16- or 32-bit floats). Since decode is **memory-bound**, halving the bits halves the **bytes streamed per token**, so throughput roughly **doubles** even though the arithmetic units were never the bottleneck. Two bonuses: the model fits in less **HBM** (or on fewer GPUs), and modern **tensor cores** have faster low-precision paths.

**The tell — the catch:** accuracy loss, fought with **per-channel scales** (a separate scale factor per weight channel), **outlier handling** (a few activations carry extreme values that wreck naive scaling), and **quantization-aware training** (training the model to tolerate the rounding). Quant helps disproportionately *because* the win is fewer bytes moved, not fewer FLOPs.

prompt: What is the KV cache, what does it cost, and what does it save?

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Attention (the KV cache)

reveal:
Gist: the **KV cache** stores the keys and values of past tokens so each new token does not have to recompute them — trading memory for a big cut in compute.

During **autoregressive** generation (one token at a time), each new token attends to all previous tokens; recomputing every prior token's **keys and values** each step would be **quadratic** work. The KV cache saves those past K and V, so each step only computes K and V for the **new** token — turning O(n²) recomputation into O(n) lookup. The cost is memory that grows **linearly** with sequence length × batch × layers × heads, and at long context it often **exceeds the model weights themselves**.

**The tell:** that is why **PagedAttention** (in vLLM) manages the cache like operating-system virtual memory, and why **grouped-query attention** shrinks it by sharing K/V across query heads — the KV cache, not the weights, is usually what caps your batch size.

prompt: Why does batching help inference throughput, and what is continuous batching?

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Ops:Byte Ratio and Arithmetic Intensity (batching)

reveal:
Gist: **batching** lets one weight load serve many requests at once, which is what pushes inference off its memory bottleneck; **continuous batching** keeps that batch full at all times.

Loading a weight matrix once and applying it to **B** sequences turns a matrix-**vector** product (one token) into a matrix-**matrix** product (B tokens), raising **arithmetic intensity** (math per byte) roughly **B×** and sliding you rightward on the roofline toward **compute-bound**. **Static** batching wastes capacity: every request in the batch must finish together, so short generations idle while the longest one runs. **Continuous (in-flight) batching** instead evicts finished sequences and admits new ones at *each* decoding step, keeping the batch full.

**The tell:** continuous batching typically **multiplies throughput several-fold at the same latency** — the batch is never left half-empty waiting on stragglers.

prompt: Distinguish data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism. What does each cost in communication?

src.ref: Ch.5 How to Parallelize a Transformer for Training

reveal:
Gist: three ways to split a model across GPUs — **data**, **tensor**, and **pipeline** parallelism — and each pays a different communication bill.

**Data parallelism** replicates the whole model on each GPU and splits the **batch**; every step ends with an **all-reduce** of gradients (a collective that sums each GPU's gradients and shares the result) — traffic proportional to **model size**, once per step. **Tensor parallelism** splits individual weight **matrices** across GPUs, so a single layer's forward pass needs an all-reduce of **activations** — very frequent and latency-sensitive, so it is normally kept **within one node** over the fast **NVLink** interconnect. **Pipeline parallelism** puts different **layers** on different GPUs and communicates activations only at the **stage boundaries** — cheap on bandwidth, but it introduces the **pipeline bubble** (stages idle waiting for work), softened by splitting the batch into **micro-batches**.

**The tell:** the three trade differently, so large runs combine all of them — **3D parallelism**. Match the split to its cost: data → gradient all-reduce; tensor → activation all-reduce (keep it on NVLink); pipeline → cheap but bubbly.

prompt: What is a systolic array and how does a TPU differ from a GPU architecturally?

src.ref: Ch.2 How to Think About TPUs — the MXU systolic array

reveal:
Gist: a **systolic array** is a grid of tiny multiply-add cells that pass data hand-to-hand, so one memory read feeds many operations; a **TPU** is a chip built around one big such array.

In a systolic array, data flows **rhythmically** between neighbouring cells (the name is from 'systole,' a heartbeat): each **MAC cell** (multiply-accumulate) takes operands from its neighbours, does one multiply-add, and passes them along. Because operands travel **directly cell-to-cell**, a single memory read is reused across many computations — huge data reuse with almost no register-file or cache traffic. A **TPU** (Tensor Processing Unit) is built around one large matrix unit like this, plus big on-chip memory and a **simpler control model**, optimized narrowly for dense **matmul**.

**The tell — the contrast:** a **GPU** is a more general many-core **SIMT** machine (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) with caches and flexible branching, so it handles a far wider range of workloads — at lower peak matmul efficiency than a TPU. Systolic array = maximize reuse of each fetched operand.

prompt: Why do Cerebras and Tenstorrent emphasize on-chip SRAM? State the core economic argument.

src.ref: Ch.3 Hardware — Other Datacenter Accelerators

reveal:
Gist: **Cerebras** and **Tenstorrent** bet on keeping weights in on-chip **SRAM** because fetching a byte from off-chip memory costs far more than reading it from on-chip — and inference is all about fetching weights.

Moving a byte from off-chip **DRAM** (the **HBM**, high-bandwidth memory) costs roughly **two orders of magnitude** more energy — and far more latency — than reading it from on-chip **SRAM** (the fast static memory right next to the compute). Since inference is dominated by **streaming weights**, the machine's speed is set by **memory bandwidth**, not FLOPs. Put the weights in SRAM **next to** the compute and that expensive trip disappears — **Cerebras** does it with a **wafer-scale** chip; **Tenstorrent** with **distributed SRAM per core**.

**The tell — the economic argument:** HBM is **expensive and supply-constrained**, so an architecture that needs less of it can undercut GPU pricing while running *faster* on memory-bound work. On-chip SRAM is a bet against the HBM bottleneck.

prompt: State Amdahl's law and what it implies about GPU acceleration of a mixed workload.

src.ref: Ch.1 Introduction — Amdahl's law and the limits of speedup

reveal:
Gist: **Amdahl's law** says the serial part of your program caps your speedup no matter how fast the parallel part gets.

The formula: **Speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/s)**, where **p** is the fraction of runtime that can be parallelized and **s** is the speedup achieved on that portion. The consequence is brutal: if just **10%** of your runtime is inherently **serial** (p = 0.9), the maximum possible speedup is **10×** — even with an infinitely fast GPU (s → ∞). For a mixed workload this means the **bottleneck migrates**: accelerate the matmul and suddenly data loading, Python overhead, or the CPU→GPU transfer dominates.

**The tell:** this is why you **profile before optimizing**, and why end-to-end wins usually come from **removing serial sections**, not from making the already-parallel part even faster.

prompt: What is the cost of CPU–GPU data transfer and what techniques reduce it?

src.ref: Ch.20 Programming a heterogeneous computing cluster — host–device transfer, pinned memory, streams

reveal:
Gist: getting data across the **PCIe** bus between CPU and GPU is roughly 10× slower than the GPU's own memory, so transfers can quietly become the bottleneck.

**PCIe** (the CPU–GPU interconnect) bandwidth is about an **order of magnitude below** on-device **HBM** bandwidth, so a kernel that is fast on paper can be dominated by just getting data to it. The fixes: use **pinned** (page-locked) host memory so the **DMA engine** (the copy hardware) can transfer without an extra staging step; **overlap** transfer and compute using **CUDA streams** (independent queues of work) so the next batch uploads while the current one computes; keep data **resident** on the device across many kernels instead of round-tripping; and **batch** many small transfers into one large one.

**The tell:** reach for **unified/managed memory** (a single address space the runtime pages automatically) only where the access pattern justifies it — its convenience can hide expensive transfers. The through-line: move data less, and overlap the moves you cannot avoid.

prompt: How do you tell whether a GPU kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound in practice?

src.ref: Ch.6 Performance considerations — analysis and profiling

reveal:
Gist: to find a kernel's bottleneck, measure how close it gets to the hardware's two ceilings — peak FLOPs and peak memory bandwidth — and whichever it is hugging is your bound.

Measure **achieved FLOPs** and **achieved memory bandwidth**, then compare each to the hardware **peak**; the one nearer its ceiling is the limit. **Nsight Compute** (NVIDIA's kernel profiler) reports exactly this — **SM throughput** vs **DRAM throughput** — and often labels the bound directly. A quick analytical check first: compute **arithmetic intensity** by hand (total FLOPs ÷ bytes moved) and compare it to the device's **FLOPs-per-byte** ratio (~**100+** on modern GPUs); below that ratio you are **memory-bound**.

**The tell — the often-missed third case:** if *neither* achieved number is near peak, you are **latency-bound** — too few **warps** to hide memory latency, or a dependency chain serializing the work. Do not optimize the math on a memory-bound kernel; confirm the bound first.

prompt: Back-of-envelope: how much VRAM do the WEIGHTS of an N-billion-parameter model take, and how does dtype change it? Work 7B and 70B across fp16, int8, int4.

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Calculating Inference Bottlenecks (weight memory)

reveal:
Gist: a model's **weights** take **params × bytes-per-param** of VRAM, and the data type sets the bytes — so in fp16 the rule of thumb is **GB ≈ 2 × the parameter count in billions**.

Bytes per parameter by **dtype**: **fp32** = 4, **fp16/bf16** = 2, **fp8/int8** = 1, **int4** = 0.5. So in fp16, **weight GB ≈ 2 × params(B)**: a **7B** model → **14 GB**, a **70B** → **140 GB**. Halve the bits and you halve the footprint — 70B is **70 GB** at int8 and **35 GB** at int4.

**The tell:** this one number already tells you the GPU count. 70B in fp16 (140 GB) does **not** fit a single **80 GB H100**, but 70B at int4 (35 GB) fits with room to spare — which is the whole point of quantizing for deployment. Bytes-per-param × params, then check it against your GPU's HBM.

prompt: You are sizing a GPU to serve a model. List every term in the VRAM budget and how you decide whether it fits. What is easy to forget?

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Calculating Inference Bottlenecks (the VRAM budget)

reveal:
Gist: the VRAM a served model needs is **weights + KV cache + activations + overhead** — and the term people forget, the KV cache, is often what actually decides whether it fits.

**Weights** = params × bytes-per-param (fixed once you pick the dtype). The **KV cache** scales with **batch × sequence length** and at long context / high batch can **exceed the weights** (see the KV-cache formula). **Activations** are transient — modest during **decode** but larger during **prefill**, proportional to prompt length × batch. **Overhead** is the **CUDA context**, framework buffers, and allocator **fragmentation** — budget ~**1–2 GB** plus ~**10–20% headroom**.

**The tell — the fit check:** pick your max batch and context, sum the four terms, and confirm the total lands under **HBM capacity** with headroom. The KV term — not the weights — usually caps your achievable batch size, so size for it first.

prompt: Write the KV-cache size formula and compute it for Llama-2-7B (32 layers, hidden 4096, MHA, fp16) at 4096 tokens. Compare to the weights and show why it dominates long context.

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Attention (KV cache sizing)

reveal:
Gist: the KV cache costs **~0.5 MiB per token** for a 7B model — and because it grows with sequence × batch, at long context it dwarfs the 14 GB of weights.

The formula: **KV bytes = 2 (one K, one V) × layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × seq × batch × bytes-per-element.** With standard **MHA** (multi-head attention), n_kv_heads × head_dim equals the hidden size, so it simplifies to **2 × layers × hidden × seq × batch × bytes**. For **Llama-2-7B** (32 layers, hidden 4096, fp16 = 2 bytes): 2 × 32 × 4096 × 2 = **0.5 MiB per token**. At **seq 4096** that is **2 GiB** for one sequence; at **batch 32**, about **64 GiB** — far past the **14 GB** of weights.

**The tell:** that linear growth in (seq × batch) is why the **KV cache, not the weights, caps how much you can batch** at long context — and why **PagedAttention** (vLLM) manages it like virtual memory and **GQA** shrinks it at the source. Cache per token = 2 × layers × hidden × bytes; scale it by seq × batch.

prompt: Show that the arithmetic intensity of autoregressive decode is approximately equal to the batch size. What does that imply about how large a batch you need to stop being memory-bound?

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Ops:Byte Ratio and Arithmetic Intensity

reveal:
Gist: in single-token decode, the **arithmetic intensity roughly equals the batch size** — so at batch 1 you are deeply memory-bound, and only a batch of a few hundred pushes you toward compute-bound.

Apply a weight matrix **W** (n×n) to **B** tokens: the math is **FLOPs = 2n²B**, but the bytes moved are dominated by **streaming W once = 2n²** (fp16). So **intensity = 2n²B / 2n² = B** FLOPs per byte — it *equals the batch size*. At **batch 1** that is ~1, orders of magnitude below a modern GPU's **ridge point** (~**300** FLOPs/byte), so decode is deeply **memory-bandwidth-bound** and the **tensor cores** sit idle.

**The tell:** to reach compute-bound you need **B on the order of a few hundred**, and every batched request rides in on weights you already had to load. That is exactly why **batching multiplies decode throughput at near-constant latency** — until the batch is big enough to hit the compute roofline.

prompt: What is the roofline 'ridge point', how do you compute it for an H100, and where does batch-1 LLM decode land relative to it?

src.ref: Ch.1 Roofline Analysis — peak arithmetic intensity (the ridge point)

reveal:
Gist: the **ridge point** is the arithmetic intensity where a GPU stops being memory-limited and starts being compute-limited — for an H100 it is around **300 FLOPs per byte**, and batch-1 decode sits far to the left of it.

It is the intensity where the roofline's two roofs cross: **ridge = peak FLOPs ÷ peak memory bandwidth**. Below it you are **memory-bound**; above it **compute-bound**. For an **H100 SXM**: ~**990 TFLOP/s** dense fp16 ÷ ~**3.35 TB/s** HBM3 ≈ **~295 FLOPs/byte**. So a kernel must reuse each byte ~**300 times** to saturate the math units. **Batch-1 decode** has intensity ~**1–2** — roughly **150× to the left** of the ridge — so it runs at a tiny fraction of peak FLOPs, its speed set purely by **HBM bandwidth**.

**The tell:** that ~150× gap is the headroom every inference trick — **batching**, **quantization**, **speculative decoding** — is trying to claw back. Ridge = peak-FLOPs ÷ peak-bandwidth; reuse each byte that many times, or you are memory-bound.

prompt: Prefill and decode are two different bottlenecks. Characterize each (resource bound, latency metric), explain why co-locating them on one GPU hurts, and what disaggregation does.

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — LLM Inference Bottlenecks (prefill vs decode)

reveal:
Gist: inference has **two** bottlenecks — **prefill** is compute-bound and sets how fast the first token appears; **decode** is memory-bound and sets how fast the rest stream out. Running both on one GPU makes them fight.

**Prefill** processes the whole prompt at once — a big matmul over N tokens with **high arithmetic intensity** — so it is **compute-bound** and sets **TTFT** (Time-To-First-Token), scaling with prompt length. **Decode** emits one token per step, streaming all weights to make a single token — **memory-bandwidth-bound**, and it sets **TPOT** (Time-Per-Output-Token). On a shared GPU they interfere: a long prefill **monopolizes the compute units** and stalls in-flight decodes, spiking **tail latency**.

**The tell:** **disaggregated serving** (**DistServe**, **Splitwise**) runs prefill on one GPU pool and decode on another, shipping the **KV cache** between them — so each phase is batched and scaled for its own bottleneck, and a burst of long prompts no longer jitters everyone's token stream. Two phases, two bounds, two metrics (TTFT vs TPOT) — separate them.

prompt: Explain speculative decoding and, using the roofline, why it accelerates a MEMORY-bound decode. What determines the speedup, and what is the failure mode?

src.ref: Ch.5 Techniques — Speculative Decoding (draft-target)

reveal:
Gist: **speculative decoding** speeds up memory-bound decode by having a small **draft** model guess several tokens, then letting the big **target** model check them all in one pass — turning several slow steps into one.

A cheap **draft** model autoregressively proposes **γ** tokens; the big **target** model then verifies all **γ+1** in a **single forward pass** (parallel, like a mini-prefill), accepting the longest prefix that matches its own distribution and correcting the first mismatch. It wins because decode is **bandwidth-bound**: one streaming of the target's weights now yields several tokens instead of one, raising **arithmetic intensity** and amortizing the memory load — several memory-bound steps become one more compute-dense step, **output-identical** to ordinary greedy/sampled target decoding.

**The tell:** speedup grows with the **acceptance rate α** — expected tokens per verify step ≈ **(1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α)** (the accepted prefix plus one bonus token) — typically **2–3×**. The failure mode: a draft that is too slow or poorly aligned means low α — wasted draft work and little gain. One weight-load, many tokens, same output.

prompt: Distinguish weight-only from weight-plus-activation quantization. Which one speeds up memory-bound decode, which is needed for compute-bound prefill, and why are activations harder to quantize?

src.ref: Ch.5 Techniques — Quantization Approaches (weight-only vs activation)

reveal:
Gist: **weight-only** quantization speeds up **decode** (a memory problem); to speed up **prefill** (a compute problem) you must **also** quantize the **activations** — and activations are the hard part.

**Weight-only** quant (**GPTQ**, **AWQ**; INT4/INT8 weights, fp16 activations, **dequantized on the fly**) shrinks the bytes streamed per token, so it directly speeds **memory-bound decode** and lets the model fit on fewer GPUs — but the matmul still runs in **fp16** after dequant, so it does little for **compute-bound prefill** and adds dequant overhead. To accelerate the *compute*, you must **also quantize activations** (INT8 on both, or **FP8**) so the low-precision **tensor cores** do the math. The catch: activations carry **outliers** — a few channels with extreme magnitudes — that wreck naive scaling.

**The tell:** that is why **SmoothQuant** migrates scale from activations into the weights, and why **per-token / per-channel** scales are used. **FP8 (E4M3)** is popular because its floating range tolerates those outliers better than INT8 and is native on **Hopper**. Weight-only → decode; weight+activation → prefill; activations are hard because of outliers.

prompt: A 70B model in fp16 is 140 GB — too big for one 80 GB GPU. Compare tensor vs pipeline parallelism for SERVING it: what each splits, its per-token communication cost, and its latency implication.

src.ref: Ch.5 Techniques — Model Parallelism (tensor vs pipeline)

reveal:
Gist: to serve a **70B fp16 model (140 GB)** that will not fit one **80 GB** GPU, **tensor** parallelism splits every matrix (low latency, but must stay inside a node) while **pipeline** parallelism splits layer-ranges (cheap comms, but no latency win).

**Tensor parallelism** shards each weight **matrix** (and the attention heads, hence the **KV cache**) across GPUs, so every layer needs an **all-reduce of activations** — roughly two per transformer block, per forward pass. That traffic is frequent and latency-critical, so TP is kept **within a node** over **NVLink**; it lowers per-GPU memory *and* per-token latency, but only scales well to a node's worth of GPUs. **Pipeline parallelism** assigns contiguous **layer ranges** to different GPUs and ships activations only at **stage boundaries** — tiny bandwidth, tolerant of slower cross-node links — but it **does not cut single-request latency** (a token still traverses all stages in order) and it adds **pipeline bubbles**.

**The tell — practical serving:** **TP within a node** for latency, then add **PP across nodes** only when the model exceeds one node. TP = frequent activation all-reduce (needs NVLink); PP = cheap but latency-neutral and bubbly.

prompt: How do multi-query and grouped-query attention shrink the KV cache, and by exactly what factor? Use Llama-2-70B as the example.

src.ref: Ch.2 Models — Attention (grouped-query / multi-query attention)

reveal:
Gist: the KV cache grows with the number of **KV heads**, not query heads — so **grouped-query attention** shrinks it by exactly **n_heads / n_kv_heads**, which is **8×** for Llama-2-70B.

**MHA** (multi-head attention) gives every **query head** its own K/V pair (n_kv_heads = n_heads). **MQA** (multi-query attention) collapses all of them to a **single** shared K/V head. **GQA** (grouped-query attention) is the middle ground — **G groups** of query heads each share one K/V head. So the cache shrinks by exactly **n_heads / n_kv_heads**. **Llama-2-70B** has **64 query heads** but only **8 KV heads** → an **8× smaller** KV cache, with negligible quality loss.

**The tell:** that reduction buys **longer context or bigger batches** within the same HBM — which is why essentially every modern long-context model ships with **GQA**. Cache scales with KV heads; cut them, cut the cache.
